newsitem.title: GERMANY: Spymaster Wolf on trial for Cold War kidnappings.
newsitem.headline: Spymaster Wolf on trial for Cold War kidnappings.

text.p: Legendary East German spymaster Markus Wolf, already cleared of treason charges, goes on trial for the second time on Tuesday, this time accused of Cold War kidnappings that are the stuff of classic spy thrillers.

The trial is a last bid by prosecutors to bring Wolf to book after the supreme court overturned an earlier conviction for treason. It said he could not be convicted for spying from East Berlin on what was then a foreign country -- West Germany.

This time the charges focus on more mundane underworld thuggery, but the wily 73-year-old who for decades was "the man without a face" to Western intelligence services again says he is the target of a political prosecution.

"In the first trial I was supposed to be made into a symbol of East German evil because I allegedly wanted to destabilise West Germany with my intelligence service," he told Monday's edition of the news weekly Der Spiegel.
"Since the Constitutional Court didn't play along, they're trying to make an example of me in a different way...In my case, the winners of the Cold War are showing themselves to be very bad losers."
It is a point Wolf made before his first trial, when he accused former West Germany of trying to take revenge for more than three decades of spectacular intelligence coups.

These ranged from the planting of "mole" Guenter Guillaume inside the office of Chancellor Willy Brandt -- forcing Brandt to resign in 1974 -- to the 10-year-long infiltration of NATO headquarters by Rainer Rupp, the spy known as "Topaz".

In the latest case, to avoid falling foul of the Constitutional Court, prosecutors have charged Wolf with offences which were also crimes under East German law: abduction, coercion and causing bodily harm.

Wolf, who has appeared almost to taunt German prosecutors with his suave, gently smiling manner and his appearances as book author and chat show guest, says this only reflects another double standard.
"Even if the allegations were true, they are charges you could bring against almost any intelligence operative in East or West," he said.
The three cases from the height of the Cold War now being tried in Duesseldorf's high-security courtroom could certainly have figured in any respectable spy thriller.

In 1962 an officer of the Ministry for State Security -- the feared East German secret police whose foreign intelligence operation Wolf founded and ran for three decades -- was demoted over a love affair which his superiors disapproved of.
The officer, Walter Thraene, fled to Austria. But Stasi officers lured him and his girlfriend to a hideout, beat him unconscious and spirited them back to East Berlin.
Thraene spent over 10 years in jail, his girlfriend three.
Wolf denies having known of that operation, but his signature does appear on the 1955 order to try to recruit Christa Trapp, a German translator at the U.S. High Commission in West Berlin.
Trapp was abducted to East Berlin but refused to sign up as a spy and was sent home the next day.

And Wolf makes no secret of having ordered the detention in 1959 on fabricated charges of Georg Angerer, an East German typesetter who worked in Nazi-occupied Norway in World War Two as interpreter for the Gestapo secret police.
The aim was to make Angerer sign defamatory statements about Brandt, then mayor of West Berlin, who spent some time in Norway during the war.

Wolf says he genuinely suspected that Brandt had been a Gestapo agent. "Then the suspicion could not be confirmed, and we dropped the matter." Angerer was released after six months -- according to the prosecution, a broken man. REUTER
